BUDDING BANDSMEN--WOODLAND RESERVATION OF MUSIC.

The extensive grounds of Kneller Hall, Hounslow frequently give forth weird noises, which are produced by musicians hidden among the trees, practicing notes on a variety of instruments. The hidden musicians are boys and men of the British Army School of Music, who are being trained as Army bandsmen, and each pupil is given a space of 15 square yards to practice on his instrument.
Photo shows. Young pupils learning the French horn.

WHAT SHIP DID CENTURION SINK?

What vessel did the new battleship Centurion sink in the disastrous collision on Tuesday morning? How many lives are lost and what is their nationality? All these questions remain to be answered, and so far the only clue is contained in an inscription on a lamp belonging to the steamship that went down with all hands off Portland Bill.
The Centurion went from Plymouth Sound into Devonport Harbour yesterday morning. As soon as possible she will be placed in dock for survey and repairs. The bows are very badly damaged.
It was yesterday believed that the unknown vessel was the steamer Osprey, of Waterford, but later messages reported this vessel making for Weymouth.
Meanwhile a telegram received from the Administration states:—
The Centurion reports that a steamer's port oil bow light, found on the Centurion's net-shelf is marked "J. H. Peters and Bey, Hamburg, 1668."

FIVE MISSING AFTER COLLISION.

ONE MAN RAILWAY
STRIKE ENDING.

Struck amidships in a collision with the steam trawler Cyelse last night in Milford Haven, the steam trawler Eagle, with her owner aboard, sank like a stone, and at a late hour five of her crew were reported to be missing.
One man of the Eagle's crew was picked up by a boat lowered from the Cyelse and three other clamboured over her stern.

LAMPLIGHT MURDER.
Agra, Dec. 11.—The trial of Lieutenant Clark and Mrs. Fulham, who are charged with the murder of Mrs. Clark, the former's wife, was resumed this morning, when Miss Clark was further examined.

James Roch, owner; George Sturley, skipper; George Hicks, deck hand; and Archie Sturly, cook.

Reverting to the night of the murder, witness said the lamp in the room was very low and she was unable to recognise the assailant, and could not identify him as the prisoner Budhu. When witness was describing the details of the assault to her father on the following day for a report to the police he said: "Keep quiet; I will give my own wording."
Her father, witness continued, used to abuse her mother most violently. On one occasion when she (Mrs. Clark) objected to his going out with Mrs. Fulham her father threatened to kick her.

The next witness was Bibu, Lieutenant Clark's former servant, who testified that Clark called him to his bedroom and gave him three powders to be put into the Mem Sahib's tea, and promised him fifty rupees when he had done it.
When Clark went out witness gave the powders to the Mem Sahib, and said he wanted to leave immediately. The Mem Sahib paid his wages and he left.
Witness took the powders and asked what they were for. Clark replied that they were purgatives, and threatened to throttle him to death if anything leaked out.

Considerably brighter hopes of a settlement of the North-Eastern Railway strike were entertained yesterday owing to the Lord Mayor's intervention. Mr. Chester Jones, the Metropolitan Police magistrate, reached Newcastle last night to open the Home Office inquiry into the Knox case this morning.
The prevailing opinion amongst the men's representatives is that the conviction against Knox will be quashed as the result of the inquiry.

LORD MAYOR AS PEACEMAKER.
(From Our Special Correspondent.)
NEWCASTLE, Dec. 11.—As I foreshadowed last night, the strike is now drawing to a close, and a settlement is well in sight.
The Lord Mayor of Newcastle told me at five o'clock this evening that he was very hopeful of an early settlement.
"I am," said Mr. Weidner, "continuing my endeavour which I am not without hope may lead to a solution of the difficulty."

Roxy La Rocca, internationally-known harpist, who is at present making a vaudeville tour, who has just broken the world's record for endurance in harp playing. La Rocca played continuously for 10 hours and 5 minutes. He began his playing in the window of a store on Broadway in New York City and played for nine hours and fifty minutes finally being forced to stop by the police because of congestion. The harp was moved to a truck and he continued playing for another hour and fifteen minutes being forced to stop because of the numbness of his hands from the unusually cold weather in New York. He had intended continuing for a period of twenty four hours and will try again in the near future. Photo shows La Rocca and his harp. 5/11/23

THE ONE MAN BAND.

The platform at the Queen's Hall last night presented an unusual appearance. In front was a long table on which was an array of orchestral instruments amounting to 15. But only one man came on the platform to tackle this small orchestra - Capt, F.Z.Salerzweig, who is musical instructor at the military orchestra - Capt, F.Z.Salerzweig, who is musical instructor at the school, Dublin. A new feature in his instruments was a Soprano Trombone. The chief item of the programme was a grand "fantasia concerto" arranged by himself introducing a part for each of the 15 instruments in turn. The holding of a note for three minutes on the Oboe was eagerly followed with watch in hand by many members of the audience. H.D. O.P.S. Capt. Sauerzweig, with his 15 various instruments. H.D.
HEIFETZ PLATS IN THE DESERT.

Jascha Heifetz, the world-famous violinist played to a sixpenny audience at Tel Aviv, Jerusalem in order to give 10,000 persons, who were unable to afford the regular concert prices, an opportunity to hear him. He gave seven concerts in five days devoting the entire proceeds to the advancement of music education among Jews.

THE OLDEST LADY ORGANIST.

O.P.S. A recent photograph of Mrs. Kempe, who is believed to be the oldest lady organist in this country. Mrs. Kempe has been organist at Sandy Church, Beds, since 1862, and first played the organ of Biggleswade Church in 1853. She was 85 last August, when she gave an hour's organ recital at the Annual Sandy Flower Show.
